content: Frey's syndrome is an uncommon condition characterized by symptoms such as sweating, flushing, and a sensation of warmth in the preauricular and temporal regions of the face, which occur in response to gustatory stimuli. This syndrome frequently develops in individuals who have undergone procedures such as parotidectomy, submandibular gland surgery, or radical neck dissection, as well as in those who have experienced infections or traumatic injuries in the parotid region. The underlying cause of Frey's syndrome is the abnormal regrowth of facial autonomic nerve fibers. Currently, several treatment options are available for managing Frey's syndrome. These include the topical application of anticholinergic agents and antiperspirants, as well as intradermal injections of botulinum toxin. However, there is uncertainty regarding which of these treatments is the most effective and safest for patients. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of various interventions for the treatment of Frey's syndrome. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and the ICTRP. Both published and unpublished trials were considered, and the search was completed on April 28, 2014. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants diagnosed with Frey's syndrome using a clinical standard, such as Minor's starch-iodine test. Trials were eligible if they compared any intervention to no treatment (observation) or an alternative intervention, with or without a second active treatment. The primary outcomes of interest were the success rate of treatment, as determined by clinical methods such as Minor's starch-iodine test, iodine-sublimated paper histogram method, or blotting paper technique, as well as the occurrence of adverse events. A secondary outcome was the success rate as reported by patients, based on the disappearance or improvement of symptoms. Standard methodological procedures recommended by The Cochrane Collaboration were employed for data collection and analysis. However, no RCTs or quasi-RCTs meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. Although eight potentially relevant studies were retrieved, all were excluded after full-text assessment due to the lack of randomization or the absence of a confirmed diagnosis of Frey's syndrome in the study participants. One randomized controlled trial comparing two different doses of botulinum toxin in patients with Frey's syndrome was also excluded because the comparator was not an alternative treatment. As a result, the review was unable to determine the efficacy and safety of the various treatment methods for Frey's syndrome. There is an urgent need for well-designed RCTs to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions for this condition. Future studies should include patients with varying severities of Frey's syndrome and report outcomes for these groups separately. Additionally, research should explore all potentially effective treatments, such as anticholinergics, antiperspirants, and botulinum toxin, in comparison to control groups receiving alternative treatments or placebo. Subjective assessments of symptom improvement or resolution should also be considered as important outcome measures in these studies.
